paper_title: Rethinking Sequence Compression with Test-time Regression

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Sequence compression is a fundamental operation and a critical information bottleneck in efficient language and multimodal models, and yet prevailing approaches based on pooling or learned projections remain underperforming. We revisit sequence compression through the lens of test-time regression: input tokens define a regression problem whose fitted coefficients form the compressed representation. Importantly, the regression problem is learned end-to-end via backpropagation, while its coefficients are computed efficiently in closed form during the forward pass. This leads to TTR-Compressor, a general alternative to conventional pooling and projection-based compression. We evaluate TTR-Compressor as the compressor for block-wise sparse attention and the visual token merger for multimodal large language models. On block-wise sparse attention, TTR-Compressor improves RULER performance over attention-based compressors by a large margin. For visual token merging, it consistently outperforms the standard MLP merger and matches its performance with 55.6% fewer visual tokens. These results establish test-time regression as an effective primitive for sequence compression in efficient language and multimodal models.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Sequence compression is ubiquitous operation in modern efficient large model architectures (Qwen Team, 2026b; DeepSeek-AI, 2026), and yet remains surprisingly underexplored. For example, block-wise sparse attention compresses each token block into summary vector used to score and

sections.title: Technical Report
sections.content: select relevant blocks (Jiang et al., 2024; Lu et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2025), while multimodal large language models (MLLMs) merge neighboring visual features into compact tokens before feeding them into the language backbone (Wang et al., 2025; Bai et al., 2025; Team et al., 2026a). In both settings, the compressor acts as critical information bottleneck. Once information is discarded, it cannot be recovered downstream. One would expect compression to be carefully designed architectural component. However, most models rely on simple mechanisms, such as parameter-free pooling, learned projections over concatenated tokens, or at best, attention-weighted pooling. We argue that these default compressors share fundamental structural limitation, i.e., they aggregate tokens using weights that do not account for inter-token relationships. Mean pooling uses uniform weights, linear projection uses fixed position-dependent weights, and attention-weighted pooling scores each token independently. As result, redundant tokens can reinforce one another, while distinctive information is diluted. From statistical perspective, these methods primarily exploit first-order token statistics while ignoring second-order inter-token correlations, the very structure that reveals which information is redundant and which is distinctive. We introduce fundamentally different compression strategy. Rather than asking which weighted average best summarizes set of tokens, we let the tokens define regression problem and take its fitted coefficients as the summary. Specifically, our proposed TTR-Compressor, constructs selfsupervised ridge-regression problem directly from the input tokens, requiring no external labels, and uses its closed-form solution as the compressed representation. This formulation creates natural division: the outer training loop meta-learns which regression problem produces task-useful representations, while the inner closed-form solution determines how that problem should be fitted to each input. The key distinction from conventional pooling and projection arises from the Gram matrix in the regression solution. By explicitly capturing inter-token correlations, TTR-Compressor fits correlated tokens jointly, so redundant evidence has diminishing rather than purely additive influence. This input-adaptive behavior cannot be reproduced by fixed projection or additive token combination. Moreover, learning the regularizer removes the need for ridge hyperparameter tuning in large-scale pretraining. Because the compression window is typically smaller than the channel dimension (i.e., < d), we solve the dual problem with an efficient Cholesky factorization. Thus, TTR-Compressor incurs minimal overhead and introduces only 2d learnable parameters per compressor, making it an effective drop-in replacement for sequence compression. We evaluate TTR-Compressor on two applications that impose fundamentally different requirements In block-wise sparse attention, the compressed summary must act as faithon compression. ful retrieval key. In this setting, TTR-Compressor consistently outperforms traditional baselines on RULER (Hsieh et al., 2024) retrieval tasks, surpassing sophisticated attention-based compressors (Hu et al., 2026) by considerable margin. In visual token merging, by contrast, the compressed summary must preserve faithful representation. Here, TTR-Compressor consistently outperforms the widely used MLP merger across diverse compression ratios, and achieves comparable performance with 55.6% fewer visual tokens. Our contributions are summarized below: novel compression framework. We introduce test-time regression framework for sequence compression, reframing token summarization as an instance-adaptive optimization problem. practical operator. We derive an efficient dual closed-form solution and eliminate hyperparameter tuning, making TTR-Compressor fully practical and scalable for large-scale pretraining. Empirical effectiveness. As drop-in component in large models, TTR-Compressor consistently outperforms conventional baselines in both block-wise sparse attention and visual token merging.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Sequence compression. Compressing sequence of tokens into single vector is fundamental operation across modern architectures, with applications ranging from multimodal token reduction (Bolya et al., 2022; Li et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2024; Cha et al., 2024; Chu et al., 2024) to block-wise sparse attention (Jiang et al., 2024; Lu et al., 2025; Gao et al., 2024; Lai et al., 2025). Existing compression operators largely fall into three paradigms: (1) parameter-free pooling, such as mean pooling; (2) concatenation followed by learned projection; and (3) attention-based compression, which summarizes tokens via attention-weighted averaging (Mohtashami & Jaggi, 2023; Yang et al., 2025b). fundamental limitation of these families is that they compute token combinations without explicitly accounting for the inter-token correlations. In contrast, TTR-Compressor

sections.title: Technical Report
sections.content: derives its representation as the solution to linear system whose Gram matrix directly encodes these correlations, providing an expressive, drop-in replacement for the operators above. Test-time regression and test-time training. The idea of adapting part of network on each input at inference time dates back to fast-weight programmers (Schmidhuber, 1992; Schlag et al., 2021) and was revived as test-time training (TTT), first for robustness under distribution shift (Sun et al., 2020) and then as sequence-modeling layers whose hidden states are small models updated by gradient descent on self-supervised loss (Sun et al., 2024; Behrouz et al., 2026b;a; Han et al., 2026). In-Place TTT (Feng et al., 2026) further extends this paradigm by directly adapting the existing MLP projection weights of pretrained Transformers. parallel line of work reinterprets linear attention and its descendants (e.g., DeltaNet (Yang et al., 2024), Gated DeltaNet (Yang et al., 2025c), Longhorn (Liu et al., 2025), Titans (Behrouz et al., 2026b)) as online regression: each layer maintains key-to-value regressor that is refined with one gradient or delta-rule step per token and read out by the query. MesaNet (von Oswald et al., 2026) pushes the inner optimization to convergence, solving the problem at every time step with conjugate gradients, while LaCT (Zhang et al., 2026) updates fast weights over large, unordered chunks to improve hardware utilization. TTR-Compressor differs from these methods in two fundamental ways. First, because compression operates independently on small, disjoint blocks without cross-block dependencies, the regression admits an efficient, exact closed-form solution via single dual solve. This avoids both iterative gradient-based inner optimization (as in TTT, ViT3, In-Place TTT, and MesaNet) and singlestep approximations (such as delta-rule updates). Second, rather than using test-time regression to produce input-dependent model weights (Bertinetto et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2020) or fast-weight memory that is subsequently queried (Schlag et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2025c; Behrouz et al., 2026b), we use regression to directly yield representation of token block. Specifically, the fitted coefficients themselves serve as the compressed representation (e.g., visual token or retrieval key). 3 JOINT SEQUENCE COMPRESSION VIA TEST-TIME REGRESSION We introduce TTR-Compressor, sequence compression operator based on test-time regression, as shown in Figure 2(a). Given sequence of token representations, TTR-Compressor constructs regression problem from the tokens and uses its fitted coefficients as the compressed representation. We first present the regression formulation of compression and specify its construction, then derive an efficient solution and describe how TTR-Compressor is learned end-to-end within model. 3.1 COMPRESSION AS TEST-TIME REGRESSION We formulate sequence compression as ridge regression (Hoerl & Kennard, 1970). The tokens in sequence provide regression observations, and the fitted regression coefficients serve as compact representation of that sequence. The regression objective encourages this representation to capture the relationships among tokens, while regularization controls the magnitude of the fitted coefficients. Given sequence = [x1, . . . , xT ] RT d, our goal is to compress its token representations into single vector Rd. We associate each token with regression key kt Rd and scalar target vt R, and define the compressed representation as: = arg min hRd 1 2 (cid:88) t= ωt (cid:0)k vt (cid:1)2 + λ h2 2, (1) where ωt 0 determines the contribution of each token and λ > 0 controls regularization. summarizes the sequence by fitting the key-target relationships across its tokens. The regression target vt is meta-learned through the task loss, while the regression itself is constructed and solved for each input sequence during both training and inference. Overall, we are solving bi-level optimization, where the outer objective is the task loss that finds the task-useful target vt, and the inner objective is the test-time regression Eq. 1 that solves the compressed representation h. sections.title: 4 UNDERSTANDING TTR-COMPRESSOR
sections.content: The learning process of TTR-Compressor can be decomposed into two distinct mechanisms: outerloop training learns which regression problem is useful for compression, while the inner solution adapts the compressed representation to the current inputs statistics. We examine them separately. 4.1 TASK-SUPERVISED LEARNING OF THE COMPRESSION OBJECTIVE The regression objective is not prescribed independently of the task. sections.title: 5 APPLICATIONS AND EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS
sections.content: We evaluate TTR-Compressor in two settings: block-wise sparse attention for efficient language modeling, where compressed representations guide context selection, and visual token merging for efficient multimodal understanding, where they serve as the visual input to the language backbone. 5.1 BLOCK-WISE SPARSE ATTENTION Architecture and Baselines. Block-wise sparse attention partitions the context into blocks, scores their compressed representations against each query, and attends to tokens in selected blocks alongside local window. The compressor therefore determines which distant information remains accessible: an uninformative summary can prevent relevant block from being selected, regardless of the quality of its individual token representations. We adopt HiLS-Attention (Hu et al., 2026) as base framework and vary only the compressor. HiLSAttention has three effective architectural components: hierarchical softmax attention, which combines within-block attention with learned block-level weights; low-rank query calibration, which adapts queries for scoring compressed representations; and HoPE, which applies RoPE to only subset of feature dimensions to support length extrapolation. We compare four compressors: mean pooling, concat & projection, the attention-weighted pooling used in the original HiLS-Attention, and TTR-Compressor. Full attention and sliding-window attention serve as additional references. Training and Evaluation. We train 345M-parameter language models on the FineWeb dataset (Penedo et al., 2024) with an 8K context length. Training runs for 30,000 optimization steps with global batch size of 128 sequences, corresponding to approximately 30B tokens, and uses AdamW with learning rate of 3 104. All sparse attention variants use 64-token blocks, select up to 32 distant blocks per query, and retain 512-token local window. Evaluation covers two complementary aspects. First, since queries use the compressed representations to retrieve relevant blocks, retrieval accuracy directly reflects compression quality. Following (Hatamizadeh et al., 2026), we evaluate on the single-needle (S-NIAH) and multi-key (MKNIAH) retrieval tasks from RULER (Hsieh et al., 2024), which require locating relevant information

As shown in Table 1, the choice of compressor largely determines retrieval quality. TTRCompressor outperforms all baselines by large margin, and its advantage persists when extrapolating to 16K and 32K. We attribute this to its second-order modeling: pooling and projection add up tokens independently, so the redundant context that fills most of block drowns out the few informative tokens. The Gram matrix in TTR-Compressor fits correlated tokens jointly and reduces the influence of redundant evidence, so the resulting key keeps the distinctive content that queries need to find. The convolutional variant brings further gain, reaching 12.24 points over the strongest baseline, as convolution makes the regression targets more informative and thus improves compression quality. On the benchmarks in Table 2, the evaluation contexts are too short to activate sparse attention, so these results only reflect the common-sense reasoning ability acquired during pretraining. Concat & Projection has substantially more parameters than the other compressors, which may benefit pretraining. TTR-Compressor performs well and on par with full attention. 5.2 VISUAL TOKEN MERGER Architecture and Baselines. High-resolution images produce many visual tokens, making their direct processing by language backbone expensive. Modern multimodal models therefore commonly use spatial merger to reduce the visual sequence length. widely adopted design concatenates each 2 2 group of neighboring visual features and maps it to one token through two-layer MLP (Wang et al., 2025; Bai et al., 2025; Qwen Team, 2026a; Team et al., 2026b). Longer multimodal contexts and agentic workflows with repeated visual observations further motivate stronger compression, such as 3 3 merging (Team et al., 2026a; DeepSeek-AI, 2026). We compare TTR-Compressor with the standard MLP merger. TTR-Compressor fits one regression per spatial group to compress its four or nine visual features into single vector, which two-layer MLP then projects to the language models hidden dimension. Its convolutional variant applies 3 3 depthwise convolution to the feature map before constructing the regression targets. Training and Evaluation. Results. As shown in Table 3, TTR-Compressor outperforms the MLP merger under both compression ratios. Under 2 2 merging, it raises the average from 54.93 to 55.92, and its convolutional variant further improves it to 56.03. The advantage grows under stronger 3 3 merging. The gains are most pronounced on text-rich benchmarks, where fine-grained details are easily lost during merging: under 3 3 merging, the convolutional variant improves over the MLP merger by 4.10 on OCRBench, 4.54 on InfoVQA, and 3.56 on ChartQA. On average, it outperforms the MLP merger by 2.58 points. Notably, TTR-Compressor (w/ Conv) with 3 3 merging achieves an average of 54.85, close to the 54.93 of the MLP merger with 2 2 merging, while using fewer than half as many visual tokens. We attribute the strong performance of TTR-Compressor to its secondorder modeling. The MLP merger concatenates the features in each group and maps them with fixed weights, so the mixing does not depend on how the features relate to each other. When most features in group are redundant, such as background patches, they dominate the merged token and wash out fine-grained details. In contrast, TTR-Compressor fits correlated features jointly and reduces the influence of redundant ones, so the merged token keeps the distinctive content within the group. 5.3 EFFICIENCY ANALYSIS Theoretical Complexity and Parameter Efficiency. As shown in Table 5, we find that omitting key normalization (kt = xt/xt2) precipitates collapse across retrieval tasks. We attribute this to two reasons. First, from an optimization perspective, since scalar targets are linearly generated via vt = axt, using raw keys (kt = xt) makes the static weight trivial exact fit (k vt). Consequently, the regularized solution is biased toward the fixed vector a, which weakens the instance adaptivity of test-time regression and pushes it toward an input-invariant projection. Second, from geometric and numerical viewpoint, outlier tokens with large norms dominate the Gram matrix KK, causing correlation modeling to reflect token norms rather than semantic similarity. Normalization resolves both issues at once: it breaks the trivial alignment with static parameters and prevents large-norm tokens from dominating the Gram matrix. From Static Heuristics to Anisotropic Regularization. Table 6 compares fixed regularization scalars against learnable formulations. All fixed settings outperform the baseline. Moderate values around λ = 102 perform well, while performance decreases when λ is too small (0.4364 at λ = 104) or too large (0.4238 at λ = 1). Notably, Learnable Scalar already achieves competitive average accuracy of 0.4971, demonstrating that the outer-loop task objective can reliably discover effective regularization strengths end-to-end. Extending this to coordinate-wise Learnable Diagonal (D = diag(softplus(ρ))) achieves the overall best performance. This progression shows the benefit of learning separate regularization strength for each channel: the model penalizes less useful feature directions more strongly while preserving task-critical ones.

sections.title: 6 CONCLUDING REMARKS
sections.content: In this work, we revisit sequence compression, pervasive yet often overlooked bottleneck in modern architectures, through the lens of test-time regression. Instead of relying on fixed pooling or learned projections, we formulate token compression as an instance-adaptive ridge regression problem, allowing the compressed representation to be solved directly from each input sequence. By exploiting inter-token correlations through second-order interactions, TTR-Compressor offers more expressive way to preserve sequence information while remaining lightweight and parameterefficient. Its dual-form solution further makes this formulation scalable in practice. Empirically, TTR-Compressor performs strongly across both block-wise sparse attention and multimodal token reduction, improving long-context retrieval while matching standard visual mergers with significantly fewer tokens. More broadly, our results suggest that sequence compression need not be viewed as static aggregation, but as an input-dependent inference problem that adapts to the structure of each sequence. We expect this perspective establishes test-time regression as simple, expressive, and scalable primitive for efficient foundation models.

sections.title: C IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS
sections.content: Numerical Precision. Convolution and target projection use the input precision (BF16), while regression keys and targets are cast to FP32 before the dual solve. Diagonal regularization is evaluated in FP32. We solve the positive-definite dual system using Cholesky factorization without explicitly forming an inverse, and cast the compressed representation back to the input dtype. Local Target Construction. Only the regression targets incorporate convolutional context; keys are computed from the original inputs. For language, we apply non-causal depthwise 1D convolution with kernel size 5, independently within each compression block, using two-sided zero padding of width 2. The convolution has neither bias nor activation and is initialized to the identity. For vision, we use 33 depthwise convolution. Each channel has its own spatial kernel, with no cross-channel mixing before the scalar target projection. The base compressor has 2d effective trainable parameters: for the target projection and for diagonal regularization. bias-free depthwise convolution with kernel elements adds sd parameters and O(sT d) computation. Thus, the language and vision variants require 7d and 11d parameters, respectively. Their total computational complexity remains O(T 2d) for fixed kernel sizes and d.

sections.title: D EXPERIMENTAL DETAILS
sections.content: Block-wise Sparse Attention. HiLS-Attention (Hu et al., 2026) argues that small models provide more diagnostic setting for RULERs predominantly find-and-copy tasks, as larger models may compensate for retrieval inaccuracies through greater information bandwidth. We therefore follow their setup and use 345M-parameter models to evaluate compression quality. All models use 16 Transformer layers, hidden dimension of 1,024, an FFN dimension of 4,096, and grouped-query attention with 16 query heads and 2 keyvalue heads. We use rank-64 query calibration. Training uses AdamW weight decay of 0.01 and gradient clipping at norm of 1.0; normalization parameters, biases, and embeddings are excluded from weight decay. The learning rate warms up over the first 0.7% of training and remains constant thereafter. Visual Token Merger. We use BF16 training with DeepSpeed ZeRO-1, gradient checkpointing, and maximum sequence length of 16,384 tokens. The two stages use per-device batch sizes of 4 and 1, with gradient accumulation over 4 and 8 steps, respectively. Both stages apply 3% learning-rate warmup followed by cosine decay, with minimum learning rates of 105 and 0 and weight decay of 0.01 and 0.02, respectively. For TTR-Compressor, the regression systems are solved in FP32.

sections.title: E ADDITIONAL EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS
sections.content: E.1 SCALING UP MODEL SIZE AND TRAINING BUDGET To further verify that the advantage of TTR-Compressor is not merely an artifact of the smaller-scale setting used in the main paper, we scale up both the model size and the training budget. Specifically, we train 1B-parameter model on 100B tokens and evaluate it on the same RULER subtasks across context lengths ranging from 4K to 32K. For comparison, we also scale up AttentionWeighted Poolingthe strongest baseline among all compression methods evaluated in the main papers 345M-parameter experimentsto the same 1B-parameter, 100B-token setting. As shown in Table 7, TTR-Compressor consistently outperforms the Attention-Weighted Pooling baseline across almost all context lengths and subtasks, achieving an average accuracy of 0.7996 compared to 0.735. Notably, the performance gap widens as the context length increases, indicating that TTR-Compressor scales more gracefully to longer contexts even when both model size and training budget are substantially increased relative to the main papers 345M-parameter setting. E.2 ABLATION ON THE VALUE PARAMETERIZATION Under the 3 3 compression setup, we compare five parameterizations of vt: (i) constant (vt = 1); (ii) linear (vt = axt); (iii) MLP (vt = MLP(xt)); (iv) bilinear (vt = MLP(xt)xt); and (v) their convolutional variants using local 3 3 features Conv(X)t.

Gray rows denote the TTR-Compressor configu2 + 1 As shown in Table 8, we observe: (1) Content dependence is critical: The constant target yields the lowest average (53.56), while the linear target gains +0.74, showing that regression targets must encode token content to form effective summaries. (2) Deeper heads offer marginal gains: Plain MLP matches the linear baseline (54.30), and adding convolution degrades it (53.91). Although the bilinear head slightly improves performance (54.55), its convolutional counterpart sees no further gain (54.37). (3) Spatial context outweighs head capacity: Combining local convolution with linear readout, vt = aConv(X)t, achieves the best overall score (54.85). These results indicate that value capacity is not the bottleneck; local neighborhood aggregation provides more effective inductive bias than non-linear projection. INFERENCE LATENCY OF BLOCK-WISE SPARSE ATTENTION As shown in Figure 4, all compression methods exhibit similar prefill and decode latency and substantially outperform full attention for context lengths beyond 16K tokens.
